unit.title: Secrets and dependencies
unit.description: API keys, .env files, secret scanning, key rotation, supply chain, lockfiles, automated updates, typosquatting

cards.definition: Any value that grants access: API keys, database passwords, tokens, private keys. It must never sit in the code or reach the browser.
cards.example: The Stripe secret key lives on the server only.

cards.definition: A local file of environment variables (secrets, settings) loaded at start, listed in .gitignore so it never reaches git.
cards.example: DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:pw@db.internal/shop stays on your machine and the server.

cards.definition: Automatic detection of keys and tokens in commits; GitHub and others block or flag them, and attackers run the same scans.
cards.example: A push is refused because it contains an AWS key.

cards.definition: Replacing a secret with a new one and revoking the old one, routinely or right after a possible leak.
cards.example: Revoke the leaked key, create a new one, update the server.

cards.definition: All the code you did not write but run: packages, build tools, actions, images. An attack on any link reaches you.
cards.example: A popular npm package is hijacked and ships a password stealer.

cards.definition: A file (package-lock.json, poetry.lock) that pins the exact version of every dependency, so each install gets the same reviewed code.
cards.example: npm ci installs exactly what package-lock.json lists.

cards.definition: Tools such as Dependabot or Renovate that open pull requests when a dependency has a fix, with CI to test them.
cards.example: A pull request bumps a library from 4.1.2 to 4.1.3 for a security fix.

cards.definition: Malicious packages named like popular ones (a typo away), or like names that AI assistants tend to invent.
cards.example: pip install reqeusts instead of requests.

exercises.prompt: You pushed an API key to a public GitHub repository, then deleted it in the next commit. Is that enough?
choices: No: revoke and replace the key now, it stays in the history
Yes, the key is gone now
Making the repository private is enough
Renaming the file is enough
exercises.explain: Bots scan public repositories within minutes, and the old commit still holds the key. A leaked key is burned: rotate it.

exercises.prompt: Where can a React app running in the browser keep a secret API key safely?
choices: Nowhere: go through your own server
In the .env file of the frontend build
Inside the minified JavaScript
In the localStorage of the browser
exercises.explain: Everything shipped to the browser can be read by the user. Secrets stay on a server, which calls the API for the app.

exercises.prompt: The .env file should be listed in .gitignore.
exercises.explain: True: it holds secrets and machine settings. Commit an .env.example with empty values instead, to document the variables.

exercises.prompt: What is a software supply chain attack?
choices: Malicious code arriving through a trusted dependency
A fake email asking for a password
A flood of requests on the server
A query injected into the database
exercises.explain: You can write perfect code and still ship malware through a hijacked package, build action or image.

exercises.prompt: You typed npm install reqeusts by mistake, and it installed. What is the risk?
choices: A look-alike package that may contain malware
None: npm fixes typos itself
Only a slower install
Only a duplicate of the real package
exercises.explain: Attackers register names one typo away from popular packages. Always check the exact name, its author and its downloads.

choices: Pinning exact versions, so every install gets the same code
Locking the repository against pushes
Encrypting the dependencies
Making the build use less memory
exercises.explain: Without it, a new install may pull a new, possibly compromised, version. With it, changes come only through reviewed updates.

exercises.prompt: Dependabot opens a pull request with a security fix for a library you use. Best move?
choices: Let CI run, read the changelog, merge soon
Ignore it while nothing is broken
Remove the library without checking
Turn the alerts off
exercises.explain: Security fixes are the updates attackers watch most. Tests plus a quick look make merging them low-risk.

exercises.prompt: Which line leaks the secret into the logs?
exercises.explain: Logs are copied, shared and stored for months. Never print secrets; log at most the last four characters.

exercises.prompt: An AI coding assistant can suggest a package that does not exist, and attackers register such names to trap developers.
exercises.explain: True: this is called slopsquatting. Check that a suggested package is real, maintained and widely used before installing it.

choices: Replacing a secret with a new one and revoking the old
Making a backup copy of the key
Sharing the key with the whole team
Making the key longer
exercises.explain: Rotation limits how long a leaked key stays useful. Do it right after any doubt, and on a schedule for important keys.
